newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK may need new taxes to check home prices - BOC.
newsitem.headline: HK may need new taxes to check home prices - BOC.

text.p: The long-term cure for Hong Kong's high property prices would be to increase housing supply, but new taxes could also be imposed to check speculation, the Bank of China said in a quarterly report published on Wednesday.

"Raising housing supply will get to the root of Hong Kong's real estate problem, and if necessary it should be supplemented with measures to curb speculation and to regulate the market," the bank's economic research division in Hong Kong said.
The government could consider following other markets' practice of using taxation as a mean to check excessive fluctuation in property prices.
In a report titled "Bringing Hong Kong's property market onto a long-term steady development track", the bank did not specify what kind of tax measures should be considered.

The bank's economists proposed increasing land supply, greater transparency of government policy, lengthening the period in which developers may market and sell unfinished flats and quickening redevelopment of old urban areas as some of the solutions to Hong Kong's housing problems.
Property analysts differ on what the new Hong Kong government should do, but some have suggested a sales tax or a capital gains tax to reign in speculation.
Hong Kong's future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa has said problems in the territory's pricey residential property market would be at the top of his agenda after he assumed his position on July 1.
China will regain sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1.
Tung has already commissioned a report from property surveyor C.Y. Leung to study Hong Kong's housing problems.

"People generally expect the Special Administration Region government to achieve better regulation of the (property) market and curb speculation, while at the same time safeguarding free market operations," the report said.
It also said Hong Kong's real estate market was crucial to the territory's economy development.

"If property prices fall drastically, it will affect the stability of the finance sector and property-related activities, dampen government revenue and threaten Hong Kong's low tax system," the bank warned.
